records.why: The lesson (and Lessons 7 and 8) rely on the formula ½ab sin C being taught in Sub-Strand 2.4 and on learners using sin on a calculator. I could not confirm what Sub-Strand 2.4 covers for Essential Mathematics, so I added a degree-mode check, a fallback (give the rule; the 60° case can be checked with the equilateral-triangle area) and removed the vague 'Trigonometry unit' call. Check: (√3/4) × 196 = 0.43301 × 196 = 84.87 cm², equal to ½ × 196 × sin 60° = 98 × 0.8660 = 84.87 cm². Teacher decision: confirm that your class has met sin C in Sub-Strand 2.4; if not, keep the fallback.

If no response, or if sin has not been met in Sub-Strand 2.4 for your class (check your scheme of work), give the formula as a rule, and for the 60° case confirm it with the equilateral-triangle area (√3/4) × 14² ≈ 84.87 cm²:

records.value:
Lesson 1 — PREDICT/OBSERVE: Anchoring Phenomenon Launch, Sector Intuition at Wakulima Market (40 min)
Learners rank four watermelon slices of the same radius but different central angles (30°, 90°, 120°, 180°, each cut from a same-size melon), count grid squares to estimate their areas (r = 7 cm: about 13, 38, 51 and 77 cm²), notice that area grows with the central angle, build the Driving Question Board (DQB) and draw a first model.

Lesson 2 — Deriving the Sector Area Formula (40 min)
Learners tile four 90° sectors onto a circle of radius 14 cm, see a sector as θ/360 of the circle, write A = (θ/360) × πr², and use it on 45°, 90° and 135° slices. They update the DQB and the model.

Lesson 3 — Investigating Sector Area with Cut-Outs (80 min)
Groups cut sectors with a fixed radius and different angles, then a fixed angle and different radii (4, 8, 10 cm), confirm that area is proportional to θ and to r², and judge whether the vendor's 90° and 180° cuts are fair.

Lesson 4 — Cutting Watermelon Fairly: Applying the Sector Formula (40 min)
Groups cut five sectors from circles of radius 7 cm, build a class table, state the formula in words and apply it to a 45° ugali-cake slice; the Kisumu door-sweep is take-home practice.

Lesson 5 — From Wedge to Segment (40 min)
Learners predict, then see that a segment is a sector minus a triangle, learn the triangle area ½r²sinθ, derive A = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ and use it on a 90° piece of a 14 cm melon.

Lesson 6 — Applying the Sector Formula: Watermelon Wedges to Irrigation Arcs (80 min)
Learners practise the sector formula in graduated Kenyan contexts (a 120° watermelon slice, a school gate swinging through 75°, a 270° irrigation arc in m² and hectares), write a scaling note (double the angle, double the area; double the radius, four times the area) and complete an exit card.

Lesson 7 — Investigating Segment Area (80 min)
Groups cut a sector into a triangle and a segment, complete a data table for 60°, 90° and 120° at r = 14 cm, work examples (a watermelon, a window, a chapati) and add the segment to the model.

Lesson 8 — Segment Area, Final Explanation and Fair-Share Verdict (80 min)
Using sectors of radius 18 cm (40°, 65°, 90°, 120°), learners compute sector, triangle and segment areas, settle the Customer Complaint Card, audit the DQB, compare their Lesson 1 model with the final one, hold a gallery walk, and then complete the written Final Explanation task.

records.old:
Lesson 1 — PREDICT: Anchoring Phenomenon Launch (Sector intuition)
Learners are shown a large paper circle representing a watermelon cross-section. The teacher poses the driving question and asks learners to predict (individually, in writing) which of three drawn sectors — with angles 45°, 90°, and 135° and the same radius — has the largest area and by approximately how much. Cold-call 4 learners to share predictions; record on the Driving Question Board (DQB). Learners then discuss in pairs: what information would you need to calculate the exact area of each slice? Introduce vocabulary: sector, radius, central angle, arc.

Lesson 2 — OBSERVE: Investigating Sector Area with Cut-Outs
Learners work in groups of 4. Each group receives a printed circle (radius 7 cm), a protractor, scissors, and a ruler. Groups cut out sectors of specified angles (30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°) and arrange them side by side. They measure and record radius and angle, then calculate each sector's area as a fraction of the full circle area (πr²). Groups tabulate results and identify the pattern: Area of sector = (θ/360) × πr². Teacher circulates, asking targeted questions: "What fraction of the full circle is your 90° sector?" WAIT TIME: 30 seconds after each question before cold-calling.

Lesson 3 — EXPLAIN: Deriving and Applying the Sector Area Formula
Teacher formalises the sector area formula from the groups' findings. Learners work through three graduated examples in Kenyan contexts: (1) a 120° slice of a watermelon of radius 15 cm; (2) the area swept by a school gate of radius 1.2 m swinging through 75°; (3) a centre-pivot irrigation arc of radius 80 m through 270°. Pairs solve problems and present solutions; class evaluates. Learners update the DQB with the sector formula and one new question that has arisen.

Lesson 4 — OBSERVE: Investigating Segment Area
Learners return to their sector cut-outs. Teacher guides: "Inside this sector, there is a triangle formed by the two radii and the chord. What shape is left if we remove that triangle?" Learners cut out the triangle (base = chord, two equal sides = radius) from the sector to isolate the segment. They measure dimensions, calculate triangle area (½r²sinθ), and subtract from sector area to find segment area. Groups record the formula: Area of segment = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ. Observation schedule used for group work assessment.

Lesson 5 — EXPLAIN: Applying the Segment Area Formula
Teacher works through two fully worked examples: (1) finding the area of the segment of a circle of radius 10 cm with a chord subtending 60° at the centre (context: leather coaster waste in Kericho); (2) the area of glass NOT cleaned by a matatu wiper of radius 30 cm that sweeps 110° (the uncleaned segment near the pivot). Learners then attempt two problems independently. WAIT TIME: allow 5 minutes silent work before peer discussion. Cold-call 3 learners to present solutions on the board. Correct misconceptions around the subtraction step.

Lesson 6 — DRIVING QUESTION BOARD (DQB) Update + Mixed Practice
Learners revisit the DQB, answer questions resolved so far (sector formula, segment formula), and post new "wonder" questions. Teacher facilitates a class discussion linking back to the anchoring phenomenon: "Can we now calculate whether the mama mboga's slices are truly equal?" Learners calculate and compare three watermelon slice areas (angles 40°, 55°, 75°; radius 18 cm) and write a short justification of fairness. Introduce mixed problems combining both sector and segment in one context (e.g. total area of a decorative window panel in a Nairobi mosque).

Lesson 7 — MODEL BUILDING: Real-Life Design Task
Learners work in pairs on a design challenge: plan a circular flowerbed of radius 2 m in the school compound that is divided into 4 sector-shaped sections for different plants; one section must be exactly 25% of the total area, two sections must be equal, and the fourth section is the remainder. Learners must calculate and label the angle and area of each section. Extension: one pair calculates the area of a decorative stone path that forms a segment around the outer edge of one section. Learners produce a labelled diagram with all calculations shown.

Lesson 8 — SUMMATIVE REVIEW + MODEL PRESENTATION
Groups present their flowerbed designs and calculations to the class; peers provide structured feedback using the KICD assessment rubric criteria (sector area, segment area, application). Teacher conducts a whole-class consolidation: revisit the driving question with final answers, review the DQB for any unresolved questions, and administer a short written class activity (4 questions: 1 sector, 1 segment, 1 application, 1 multi-step). Learners reflect in their portfolios on what changed in their thinking from Lesson 1 to Lesson 8 regarding the watermelon phenomenon.

records.why: The printed rubric headings are fixed by the template, so the CBE level names (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches Expectations) are written at the start of each descriptor. Descriptor wording is unchanged otherwise.

value.criterion: Understanding of how angle and radius control area
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Clearly explains that sector area is proportional to the central angle and to r², using correct comparisons from the data (such as 30° versus 180°) and the anchoring watermelon context.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: States that angle and radius both affect area and gives a mostly correct comparison, but explanation of proportionality or the r² effect is incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Says only that bigger pieces have bigger area, or relies on the look of the pieces without mentioning angle and radius.

value.criterion: Correct use of the sector and segment formulas
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Writes both formulas correctly, explains where each part comes from (fraction θ/360 of the circle; sector minus triangle), and substitutes accurately with units.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses both formulas with only minor slips in substitution, rounding or units, and gives partial reasoning for where they come from.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Confuses sector and segment, omits the triangle subtraction, or makes major errors in substitution.

value.criterion: Accuracy of calculations and presentation of data
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: All sector, triangle and segment areas are correct, set out in a clear table with working and units, and the largest and smallest pieces are identified correctly.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Most calculations are correct and clearly set out, with one or two small errors that do not change the conclusions.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Several calculation errors, missing working or units, or a table that is incomplete or inconsistent.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Gives a clear, evidence-based recommendation to Mama Wanjiku using the calculated areas, and applies the formulas correctly to another Kenyan context such as irrigation.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives a reasonable recommendation and a correct real-life example, though links to the calculated evidence are limited.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Recommendation is vague or not supported by calculations, and the real-life example is missing or incorrect.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Describes specific changes from the Lesson 1 model to the final model, naming at least two new ideas and linking them to the driving question.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Mentions at least one idea added to the model with some link to the driving question.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives a general statement of learning without naming specific changes to the model.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the data contract allows only three level fields, so Below Expectations cannot be represented. Suggestion: decide whether the partner contract can add a fourth field; until then, treat work that does not reach Approaches Expectations as Below Expectations.

No KICD source for Essential Mathematics is available (the KICD Mathematics PDF in the project is the Core Mathematics design), so the learning outcomes, key inquiry question, core competencies, values and PCIs could not be checked against KICD wording and none was changed. Differences from the Core text that look worth a teacher's check: Core names this sub-strand 2.6 'Area of a Part of a Circle' (here it is 2.5); the Core content also covers annular sectors, and intersecting circles, which this sub-strand does not (it may be correct for Essential Mathematics but should be confirmed); and Lessons 5, 7, 8 assume Sub-Strand 2.4 taught ½ab sin C. All four outcomes (a to d) are taught and assessed in the lessons and the Final Explanation.

Storyline repetition: Lessons 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 each build the same sector idea (cut-outs of 30° to 180° at r = 7 cm appear in Lessons 1, 3 and 4; the formula is derived in Lesson 2, confirmed in Lesson 3, 'derived' again in Lesson 4 and re-derived in Lesson 6). Learners may feel they are repeating a lesson. I did not restructure the teachers' sequence. Suggestion: keep Lessons 1 to 3, make Lesson 4 pure application (different radii and the ugali and door problems) and use Lesson 6 for the three graduated contexts only.
